overview:
The year this story is pinned to, 631, falls near the end of Muhammad's life, at a moment when a religious movement that had begun as the private preaching of one man in Mecca had become the organizing force of most of the Arabian Peninsula. Muhammad had begun receiving what he and his followers understood as revelations from the one God around 610, in a Mecca whose economy and prestige turned on a polytheistic pilgrimage shrine. Rejected and eventually endangered there, he and his early community migrated in 622 to the oasis town of Yathrib, thereafter Medina — the hijra, from which Muslims still count their years. In Medina the movement acquired what it had lacked in Mecca: territory, arbitration authority over feuding clans, tax and alms structures, and an army. Mecca itself fell with little bloodshed in 630, and its shrine, the Kaaba, was stripped of its idols and absorbed into the new monotheism rather than abandoned.

What followed, in the ninth year after the hijra — roughly 630 to 631 — Muslim tradition remembers as the Year of Delegations, when tribal embassies from across Arabia came to Medina to submit, accept Islam, or negotiate terms. The picture the later sources paint of a peninsula converging on a single religious and political center is doubtless tidier than the reality, which involved coercion as much as persuasion and produced allegiances that frayed the moment Muhammad died in 632. But the direction of travel was real. Within a decade of his death, armies drawn from those same tribes had taken Syria, Egypt, Iraq, and the Iranian plateau from the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, both of them exhausted by a generation of war against each other.

Islam did not arrive in an empty religious landscape. Arabia sat between Christian Byzantium and Zoroastrian Iran, with Jewish and Christian communities inside the peninsula and long-standing trade and tribute links to both empires. The Quran addresses this world directly, treating Abraham, Moses, and Jesus as predecessors and casting Muhammad as the last in that line. The distinctive institutions a reader now associates with Islam — the five daily prayers, the fast of Ramadan, the pilgrimage to Mecca, the elaborated body of law — took their recognizable shape over the following two centuries, in the imperial cities of Damascus, Baghdad, Kufa, and Medina, in argument among scholars whose conclusions have never been fully uniform.
significance: Within roughly a century of the events of 631, a movement born among the tribes of western Arabia governed territory from the Atlantic coast of Morocco to the Indus, having permanently dislodged Byzantium from the southern Mediterranean and destroyed the Sasanian empire outright — one of the fastest and most durable political transformations in recorded history. Its consequences were not only political: Arabic became a language of administration, science, and poetry across that whole span; the Quran gave a fixed textual anchor to a legal and ethical tradition still binding on nearly two billion people; and the frontier between the Islamic world and Latin Christendom shaped centuries of war, trade, translation, and mutual borrowing. The map of the Middle East, North Africa, Central and South Asia, and the Sahel is still legible in terms of what began in these years.
coverage: This dataset holds no events at all beneath the story, and the 631–631 span is a placeholder rather than a claim about a founding date; the overview is written from general reference accounts of Muhammad's life and the early community. The deeper problem is in the record itself: almost nothing survives that was written during Muhammad's lifetime beyond the Quran, and the detailed biography — including the Year of Delegations and the chronology of the Medinan years — comes from sira and hadith compiled a century or more later, by authors with theological and communal commitments. Non-Muslim contemporary witnesses, inscriptions, and coins are fragmentary and often say little about Islam as such. Since the 1970s some scholars have argued the traditional narrative is substantially a later construction; most now work somewhere between wholesale acceptance and wholesale rejection, and specific dates before about 640 should be read as approximate.
